wishlist.name: Mr Jiu's
wishlist.notes: Try the duck. This is a Michelin-starred Chinese American restaurant in Chinatown -the original Chinatown of San Francisco. The video will show you how much care they put into that duck, and they also do amazing hot pot and cocktails.

wishlist.name: San Ho Won
wishlist.notes: Chef Corey Lee and Jeong-In Hwang's Michelin-starred Korean charcoal barbecue restaurant. The house menu is generous, the banchan and vegetables are as carefully handled as the meat, and the charcoal-grilled beef is the centerpiece. Reservations can be difficult, so book when they are released.

wishlist.name: La Taqueria
wishlist.notes: Oh my God, it might be called The Place of the Tacos, but trust me, this place really knows how to make a burrito. Go for the carne asada, make it supreme, ask for extra guac if you want, and maybe ask for less beans. You will love it. You go here for the burrito -the carne asada one, amazing.

wishlist.name: Swan Oyster Depot
wishlist.notes: I recently made the line and it was totally worth it. Not only do they have amazing oysters, but always ask for a sample, but also their sashimi plates are great, as well as the clam chowder soup. Really recommend it. Worth the wait. Remember that it's cash only and get a beer.

wishlist.name: China Live
wishlist.notes: China Live made what Italy is for Italian food but for Chinese food in Chinatown. They have an amazing variety of stuff, great for groups. Try all the different dim sum. The Xiaolongbao is always a great recommendation, and it's a very big space. Not only do they have the restaurant, but there's also a speakeasy that's highly recommended.

wishlist.name: Burma Love
wishlist.notes: The Valencia branch is the best one. Find an excuse to reserve the big round table, and get there early for a drink at the bar. Tea leaf salad is a must. Menlo Park and Mint Plaza get special mention. Sister properties: Kayah by Burma Love at Chase Center, and Teakwood by Burma Love in Hayes Valley.

wishlist.name: Tony's Pizza
wishlist.notes: It's a place in San Francisco that has some awards, especially if you want to go for the Margherita or the Mozzarella one. They have seven different ovens for different styles, and they say that some of the pizzas will be sold out. I've never seen any pizza sold out, but just go early. Make the line. It's totally worth it.

wishlist.name: Rintaro
wishlist.notes: This is the beautiful izakaya that we have in town. It really cares about yakitori. And the chicken skewers are really recommended. But try everything and ask for the specials. You'll have a blast. Their sake selection is also really good. It really feels like Tokyo in the Mission.

wishlist.name: Mijoté
wishlist.notes: Modern French bistro with a California soul. The duck confit and the bone marrow with escargot are standouts. Natural wine program is exceptional. Intimate space perfect for special occasions.

wishlist.name: Lazy Bear
wishlist.notes: One of my most memorable fine-dining experiences in San Francisco. The cultured butter and bread were exceptional, but what made the meal truly special was the original shared-table dinner-party format, with everyone eating together. Lazy Bear no longer seats guests communally, but the nostalgic, hyper-seasonal tasting menu and that incredible bread and butter still make it a recommendation.

wishlist.name: Plow
wishlist.notes: Is definitely the best brunch in town. It's long hour waits on the weekends, but trust me, it's worth it. And they also have some special breakfast if they have the Chinese one, go for it. Thanks to my poblano cooks for this amazing, beautiful place in San Francisco.

wishlist.name: The Mill
wishlist.notes: Famous for thick-cut toast topped with seasonal ingredients and Four Barrel coffee. The $4 toast became a symbol of SF's artisanal food movement. Their bread from Josey Baker Bread is exceptional, and the almond butter toast with sea salt is iconic.

wishlist.name: Mensho Tokyo
wishlist.notes: This is the best ramen in town -rich, creamy broth, and it's just perfectly cooked. You will have to make a line, and of course, it's in the Tenderloin, so some people get a little bit worried about it, but trust me, totally worth it. And they have also a branch in Tokyo. I think the one in San Francisco was even first, not sure about that, but good to consider it.

wishlist.name: Octavia
wishlist.notes: This is a cozy place for dinner. Always a great selection and a good description of what New American stands for. The menu changes with the season, but it consistently feels polished, comfortable, and worth the night out.

wishlist.name: Four Kings
wishlist.notes: Cozy place that reminds me of the feeling of some izakayas, but the variety is amazing. You get Singaporean, Korean, and a lot of Taiwanese and Chinese delicatessen influences all in one dinner. Great food, great ambience, and one of the most fun meals in Chinatown.

wishlist.name: Zuni Café
wishlist.notes: Their legendary roast chicken for two with bread salad is a San Francisco institution, order it and wait the 45 minutes, it's worth it. This James Beard Award-winning restaurant has been defining California cuisine since 1979. Also try their Caesar salad and oysters.

wishlist.name: Tartine Bakery
wishlist.notes: Home to the city's most famous morning buns and country bread that launched a thousand sourdough obsessions. Their croissants are equally legendary. This bakery transformed American bread culture and remains a pilgrimage site for bakers worldwide.

wishlist.name: Noe Cafe
wishlist.notes: Known for perfectly prepared chai lattes and their avocado toast topped with hemp seeds and chili flakes. A neighborhood gem that embodies Noe Valley's village-like charm.

wishlist.name: El Chato
wishlist.notes: El Chato is that Spanish corner that brings vibes of Madrid to the Mission. Natural wine bar with great owners. Go for the tapas, the tortilla española, navajas, jamón and cheese, and ask for chatos. Trust the wine stand. On a sunny day, hang out outside.

wishlist.name: Mosto
wishlist.notes: Their tacos al pastor are amazing because they have a proper trompo, and they also have a great mezcal selection. Unfortunately, lately they are also building burgers, and despite the fact that they are trendy, I think that they are losing part of the essence that made me recommend them at the first time.

wishlist.name: Yuanbao Jiaozi
wishlist.notes: Handmade dumplings are the star. Try the pork & chive and the fish dumplings. Their hand-pulled noodles in rich broths are equally exceptional. A neighborhood favorite for authentic Northern Chinese cuisine.

wishlist.name: LoLo
wishlist.notes: Known for creative tacos like fried chicken with mole verde and their famous quesadilla with bone marrow. A modern Mexican spot that's both playful and deeply respectful of Mexican culinary traditions. Their decoration is extremely creative.

wishlist.name: Shoji
wishlist.notes: Their signature matcha soft serve and expertly prepared pour-over coffee make this a must-visit. The minimalist Japanese aesthetic creates a zen moment in busy SOMA.
wishlist.address: 140 New Montgomery St, Suite 1, San Francisco, CA 94105

wishlist.name: Dumpling Time
wishlist.notes: Watch dumpling makers through the glass window. The colorful xiao long bao (soup dumplings) and the King-Dum (massive pork & shrimp dumpling) are Instagram-famous for good reason. Modern take on dim sum classics.

wishlist.name: Kingdom of Dumplings
wishlist.notes: No-frills spot for authentic Beijing-style dumplings. Their lamb & cumin dumplings and the hand-pulled biang biang noodles are exceptional. Cash only, worth the trek to the Richmond.

wishlist.name: 4505 Burgers & BBQ
wishlist.notes: Founded by champion pitmaster Ryan Farr. The 'Best Damn Cheeseburger' lives up to its name, and the brisket is properly smoked for 18 hours. Their picnic-style outdoor seating captures SF's casual dining spirit.

wishlist.name: Cantoo Latin Asian Rotisserie
wishlist.notes: Venezuelan and Chinese fusion with a lovely history coming from Venezuela and Panama to the Tenderloin. Will always honor their 9 dollar rice and chicken dish. A unique blend of Latin American and Asian flavors that tells the story of migration and cultural fusion in San Francisco.

wishlist.name: Burma Super Star
wishlist.notes: The tea leaf salad is legendary, fermented tea leaves with nuts and seeds create umami magic. Rainbow salad and coconut rice are also must-orders. Expect a wait; this place introduced Burmese cuisine to many Americans.

wishlist.name: Piccino
wishlist.notes: Wood-fired pizzas with creative California toppings and excellent natural wines. Weekend brunch is exceptional. Their backyard garden patio is one of SF's best outdoor dining spots.

wishlist.name: Shizen
wishlist.notes: Vegan sushi that converts carnivores. The spicy tuna (made from tomatoes) and the candied walnut & quinoa roll are revelations. Proof that plant-based dining can be both sustainable and indulgent.

wishlist.name: House of Prime Rib
wishlist.notes: Old-school SF since 1949. Prime rib carved tableside from silver carts, Yorkshire pudding, and creamed spinach. The martinis are perfect. A time capsule of classic American dining.
wishlist.address: 1906 Van Ness Ave, San Francisco, CA 94109

wishlist.name: Z & Y
wishlist.notes: Explosive Sichuan flavors, the tea-smoked duck and mapo tofu will test your spice tolerance. Their 'Explosive Chili Chicken' is buried in chilies. One of the best regional Chinese restaurants in America.

wishlist.name: Kitchen Istanbul
wishlist.notes: Family-run Turkish spot. The lamb kebabs and the meze platter with house-made hummus, baba ganoush, and muhammara are exceptional. Their Turkish breakfast on weekends is an overlooked gem.

wishlist.name: Flour + Water
wishlist.notes: House-made pasta is the star. The agnolotti and the tajarin are life-changing. Neapolitan-style pizzas from the wood-fired oven are equally impressive. Reservations essential at this pasta temple.

wishlist.name: State Bird Provisions
wishlist.notes: Dim sum-style service meets California cuisine. The state bird (quail) with provisions is iconic, as are the garlic bread with burrata and the pork belly salad. James Beard Award winner that changed how Americans think about small plates.

wishlist.name: Bi-Rite Creamery
wishlist.notes: San Francisco's most beloved ice cream shop. The salted caramel is legendary, and seasonal flavors like honey lavender showcase local ingredients. Expect long lines on sunny days - it's a Mission District ritual. Their soft serve with olive oil and sea salt is a must-try.

wishlist.name: Four Barrel Coffee
wishlist.notes: Valencia Street's coffee temple with a massive roasting facility visible from the cafe. Single-origin pour-overs and expertly pulled espresso. The industrial-chic space with high ceilings and communal seating embodies Mission District coffee culture.

wishlist.name: Wise Sons Jewish Delicatessen
wishlist.notes: Modern Jewish deli serving pastrami on rye that rivals NYC's best, plus bagels, lox, and babka. Their challah French toast at brunch is exceptional. A taste of the Lower East Side in the Mission, with multiple locations across the city.

wishlist.name: Ju-ni
wishlist.notes: Intimate 12-seat omakase sushi bar from former Saison chef Geoffrey Lee. The $300+ tasting menu features pristine fish flown in from Tsukiji Market. Watching the chef's knife work up close is part of the experience. Reservations essential.

wishlist.name: Marufuku Ramen
wishlist.notes: Hakata-style tonkotsu ramen with rich pork bone broth simmered for 20+ hours. Choose your noodle firmness and richness level. The black garlic oil adds incredible depth. One of SF's best ramen shops, expect a wait.

wishlist.name: Hog Island Oyster Co.
wishlist.notes: Ferry Building institution serving oysters from their Tomales Bay farms. The grilled cheese with three artisan cheeses pairs perfectly with oysters. Views of the Bay Bridge while slurping Sweetwaters and Kumamotos. Happy hour is the best deal.

wishlist.name: Oma San Francisco Station
wishlist.notes: Located in the heart of Japantown, Oma is designed to resemble an izakaya. It is the best omakase in Japantown.
wishlist.address: 1737 Post St, Suite 337, San Francisco, CA 94115

wishlist.name: Doma Sushi
wishlist.notes: Doma remains open, but this recommendation moved with the restaurant from its former Cortland Avenue address to 433 Precita Avenue. The welcoming neighborhood setting, omakase, nigiri, salmon skin salad, and ankimo remain the reasons to go.

wishlist.name: Universal Bakery
wishlist.notes: Great breakfasts from Guatemala and pan dulce.

wishlist.name: Reem's California Mission
wishlist.notes: Arab street food meets California ingredients. Their mana'eesh (flatbreads) are baked to order in a custom oven. The za'atar with cheese and the lamb flatbread are exceptional. Owner Reem Assil creates food that tells stories of Arab heritage.

wishlist.name: Beit Rima
wishlist.notes: Modern Middle Eastern with a focus on Palestinian and Jordanian dishes. The chicken musakhan (sumac-spiced chicken with caramelized onions on flatbread) is incredible. Their hummus with lamb is a meal in itself. Cozy neighborhood spot with excellent hospitality.

wishlist.name: Balompie Cafe
wishlist.notes: Authentic pupuseria serving handmade pupusas stuffed with cheese, beans, chicharrón, or loroco. Watch them made fresh through the window. Their curtido (pickled cabbage) and salsa roja are perfect accompaniments. Cash only, incredibly affordable.

wishlist.name: Arsicault Bakery
wishlist.notes: Home of SF's best croissant - buttery, flaky perfection that regularly wins 'Best Croissant' awards. Their almond croissant and kouign-amann are equally exceptional. Arrive early, they sell out fast.

wishlist.name: Starbelly
wishlist.notes: California comfort food with a great back patio. Their fried chicken sandwich and pizzas are neighborhood favorites. Excellent brunch spot with bottomless mimosas. Dog-friendly patio.

wishlist.name: Chez Maman
wishlist.notes: Authentic French bistro with a neighborhood feel. Their moules frites and croque monsieur transport you to Paris. Great French wine selection and charming back patio.

wishlist.name: Farley's
wishlist.notes: Potrero Hill's community living room since 1989. Great coffee, fresh pastries, and a mix of locals working on laptops and families grabbing breakfast. Their outdoor seating on 18th Street is perfect for people watching. A true neighborhood institution.

wishlist.name: Trad Bone Broth
wishlist.notes: Takeout-only bone broth cafe on 24th Street: broths on tap (beef, chicken, a Korean-style Seoul Broth, and a vegetarian option) plus made-to-order savory and sweet broth drinks. Open Tue-Sun 9am-7pm, closed Mondays.

dishes_recommended.description: My usual. Brioche bun, eggs, cheddar and arugula.

dishes_recommended.name: Avocado Toast
dishes_recommended.description: Really good.

dishes_recommended.name: Coffee
dishes_recommended.description: Grab it and sit outside in the parklet.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
It's a really cool coffee shop in Noe Valley, on the Sanchez Slow Street, very child and dog friendly.

I love it. They have two branches, the other one in Mission Bay, but the one I really like is Noe Cafe in Noe Valley. They have a nice parklet, so you can really grab your coffee outside. They also have some inside tables that aren't always available, but the vibe is pretty good.

Occasionally during the week they bring a guy who sells tacos, wearing a big taco hat. It's the place where you hang out when you live in the Noe Valley area, but it's also visited by a lot of tech people and VCs.

I really recommend their sandwiches and their toast. The avocado toast is really good, and I usually get the breakfast sandwich. Other than the different coffees, they also have a selection of kombuchas, and they have a liquor license, so if you go a little later in the day you can also grab a beer. It's a great spot for a beer, and whenever there are festivities on Sanchez, the community and the ambience are really good.

Some other friends always say it's a very chill place and a great place for meetings, and I agree. It's my go-to place to have a meeting, or just to enjoy an easy coffee in Noe Valley.

Noe Cafe, the best place to have a coffee, chill and hang out with your friends in Noe Valley.

faqs.answer: Mon–Wed 7am–5pm, Thu–Sun 7am–6pm.

reviews.share_title: La Espiga: My favorite place, it really felt like home
reviews.seo_title: La Espiga, San Sebastián pintxos bar: My favorite place, it really felt like home
reviews.name: La Espiga
reviews.address: San Martzial Kalea, 48, 20006 Donostia / San Sebastián, Spain

dishes_recommended.name: Tortillita with trufa
dishes_recommended.description: Soft tortilla with truffle; start here.

dishes_recommended.name: Rollito de jamón
dishes_recommended.description: Cold pintxo of jamón rolled tight; grab it from the counter first.

dishes_recommended.name: Sardine pintxos
dishes_recommended.description: Whatever sardine they have out that day; always worth it.

dishes_recommended.name: Egg salads
dishes_recommended.description: Cold ensaladillas at the bar; easy with wine by the glass.

dishes_recommended.name: Pimentones fried
dishes_recommended.description: Hot fried peppers when you move to calientes.

dishes_recommended.name: Croquetas
dishes_recommended.description: Hot croquetas from the kitchen; ask what’s frying.

dishes_recommended.name: Albóndiga
dishes_recommended.description: Their meatball; order it with the other calientes.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
La Espiga feels like hanging out in the neighbor bar with friends and family, the service is fast, the Pintxos are really good. The wine selection is extensive, even by the glass. And they also have the claim to have started the pintxos in town. Get the Tortillita with truffles.

Opened in 1928. Luisa San Martín made the first banderillas here. The Castro family has run it for three generations. I was lucky to be introduced to some of the family through a friend, and they are just an amazing family. Three generations making pintxos and making sure that the quality is top-notch. Not only that, but the atmosphere is really good. If you notice the decoration, the floor resembles the same floor that you're gonna find in the streets of San Sebastian. There's wood on the roof of the bar that resembles a lot of trees from the Basque country, and the bar itself is made of the metal that you see in the harbor. And there's also the murals that you'll find in San Telmo Museum. So it really makes you continue being in San Sebastian while you're having some pintxos.

My recommendation is to always start with the cold ones, just look at what's available. The rollito de jamon is really good, and everything that has any sardine and their egg salads, but also ask for what they have in calientes. I have already told you about the tortillita with truffles, but they also do other tortillas, and they will also do pimentones fried, and croquetas. They also have an albondiga. And just amazing food. Everything is good. There's nothing where you're gonna miss out.

The terrace is good for friends, but I always recommend squeezing into the bar. And you can also reserve. They have a basement with fancier tables and dinner service if you wanna try their good stuff. Opening all week with a reduced menu Sundays and Mondays. And they also kinda are available until late, so pretty easy option from 10 AM till 10 PM every day of the week.

I went with friends and family, but definitely recommended for everyone. The price feels right. Of course, if you order a lot of tapas and you go to the restaurant, it might be a little bit on the upper end of pintxos, but still totally worth it.

My favorite place, it really felt like home, and I'm really glad that I was able to also understand who's behind it, how Chema and his brother run this place and keep it tight and amazing.
reviews.reservation_tip: Table reservations are by phone: +34 943 421 423. There is a basement with fancier tables and dinner service. I always recommend squeezing into the bar over the terrace.
reviews.seo_description: La Espiga, a family-run pintxos bar in San Sebastián: Tortillita with truffles, rollito de jamón, croquetas, and wine by the glass. Open 10 AM to 10 PM.

faqs.question: What should I order at La Espiga?
faqs.answer: Start with the cold pintxos on the bar: the rollito de jamón, anything with sardine, and the egg salads. Then ask what they have in calientes: the Tortillita with truffles, other tortillas, fried pimentones, croquetas, and the albóndiga.

faqs.question: Do you need a reservation at La Espiga?
faqs.answer: Not for the bar. I always recommend squeezing into the bar over the terrace. Table reservations are by phone at +34 943 421 423, including the basement with fancier tables and dinner service.

faqs.question: What are La Espiga's opening hours?
faqs.answer: It opens every day of the week, from about 10 AM to 10 PM, with a reduced menu on Sundays and Mondays. Hours change, so check before you go.

faqs.question: Is La Espiga expensive?
faqs.answer: The price feels right. If you order a lot, or eat in the restaurant downstairs, it lands on the upper end for pintxos in San Sebastián, but it is still worth it.

faqs.question: Where is La Espiga in San Sebastián?
faqs.answer: San Martzial Kalea, 48, in the Centro of San Sebastián (Donostia), a short walk from the Parte Vieja.

reviews.share_title: Sala de Despiece: I've been to three salas. I miss the original.

dishes_recommended.description: Half-kilo tomato with brine, olive oil, and basil.

dishes_recommended.name: Rolex

dishes_recommended.name: Ribs

dishes_recommended.name: Pulpo a la plancha

dishes_recommended.name: Alcachofa

dishes_recommended.name: Chuletón

dishes_recommended.name: Berenjena frita
dishes_recommended.description: Fried aubergine with the fish and pink onions.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
I've been to three salas. I miss the original. The original Calle Ponzano (2013) closed in 2024; SDD1 moved to Alonso Cano. That is why I miss the original. They really appreciate Spanish produce, they have great wines, service is always very friendly. That gigantic tomato, the Rolex and the chuleta, just beautiful presented, assembled and it tastes amazing.

My friend zordor once told me about this place and ever since I religiously visited every time that I am in Madrid. This is not the typical place that you should be said if you wanna have a local experience in Spain, but I do believe that this is the kind of place that you should visit especially if you're a tourist and you wanna see a little bit of experimentation with great produce, amazing food, and good quality of customer service.

I once went to the original Sala that has been extended now to many new branches. I have been going to some of the newer ones and they basically have more room, but keep the same atmosphere. You will be sitting at a bar most of the time even if you come with a group and there will be someone helping you with drinks, great selection of wines by the glass and also bottles, and then you start asking for some of the plates. It's recommended to have a couple of plates per person or even more.

If you really wanna do some snacks from the menu I would always get the meat. It's raw and they call it chuletón and they make it into the wrap and it's just beautiful and the presentation and everything is amazing. And then never miss the Rolex. It has fuet and it's wrapped in bacon and also some truffles and an egg and it's basically a major explosion of flavors in your mouth. They do other amazing stuff like the artichoke, which is one of my favorite ones in Spain for the texture and how they fry it. Overall their food selection and everything that they would give you is amazing. It's part show to see part of the presentation of how they finish the dishes and it's always a great place. Great to bring your friends who are being introduced to Spanish cuisine or who already have an idea of how it works and wanna get something more experimental and upscale.
reviews.reservation_tip: Choose your sala when booking through the official website. The main map points to the current SDD1 address in Chamberí; all three current restaurants are listed below.

reviews.seo_description: Sala de Despiece review, Madrid: the giant tomato, the Rolex, raw chuletón, and fried artichoke at the bar. Wines by the glass.

faqs.question: What should I order at Sala de Despiece?
faqs.answer: Never miss the Rolex. Get the chuletón, the raw beef they make into a wrap, and the giant tomato. The fried artichoke is one of my favorites in Spain for its texture. Plan on a couple of plates per person or more.

faqs.question: Which Sala de Despiece should I go to?
faqs.answer: There are three salas in Madrid: SDD1 in Chamberí (Calle de Alonso Cano, 28), SDD2 in Centro near Puerta del Sol (Calle de la Virgen de los Peligros, 8), and SDD0 in Salamanca (Calle de Ayala, 27). The original Calle Ponzano (2013) closed in 2024; SDD1 moved to Alonso Cano. I miss the original.

faqs.question: How do you book Sala de Despiece?
faqs.answer: Book through the official website, saladedespiece.com, and choose your sala (SDD1, SDD2, or SDD0) when you reserve.

faqs.question: Is Sala de Despiece a traditional Spanish restaurant?
faqs.answer: Not the typical local experience. It is great Spanish produce with some experimentation, friendly service, and part of the show is watching them finish the dishes at the counter. You sit at the bar most of the time, even with a group.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
At Arrosseria Antoni Rubies in Artesa de Lleida, stop for the rice. Order the arròs a la marinera for two, get the costillas de cordero, and leave room to look at the owner’s wall of old phones.

    I was on my way to Lleida and started looking for restaurants. I wanted a small stop and a decent menú, the way they mean it in Spain. Finding this arroceria was a beautiful surprise. A small village outside Lleida, the place was full, and it carries a Michelin Bib Gourmand. We still got a table.

    Near the table there is a collection of old smartphones. iPhones, iPods, some iPads, other phones, on display. The owner told me he has been collecting them since the early beginning of that technology.

    What was on the menu for us was cordero. The ribs were fascinating. We also had an arroz. When you get a portion for two they bring a full paella, the big pan, with shrimp and all sorts of seafood including squid. It took a while to cook and it was really lovely. Service was really good. They have ice cream for dessert and other options, but we basically went for good paella, some ribs, and a little bread.

    Very nice, cozy place. Definitely the stopover I was looking for. I would go back with a larger group and try all the different paellas, because that seems to be what they do better.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
At Geoboki Sikdang in Seoul, near Kyung Hee, come early for lunch. Order the pork, put kimchi on the charcoal, and leave room for the pork skin.

    I really believe that Korean BBQ is amazing. I saw it in many K-dramas. I've enjoyed them in K-Town in LA and in Japantown in San Francisco. But also, I'm the biggest fan of San Ho Won (reviewed here already). So this trip to Seoul I wanted locals to show me their stuff. And this is what happened.

    In California, going for Korean BBQ means mostly beef slices, a lot of wagyu and stuff they want to impress you with, bulgogi, etc. I got used to that because of K-Town in LA and the good options in the Bay Area. So when I asked friends in Seoul to impress me with Korean BBQ, I was happy to discover their passion for pork. No bulgogi, not sugar or weird marinated stuff.

    This place opens early so it's easy to get a table before it gets crowded at night with the university students nearby. We were in a university area. A local friend and tour guide helped us with the cooking and helped us understand the culture. Seems like the traditions among students, and also between coworkers, have changed since Covid. Not only that, their pork selection is really good, and the pork skin is a different texture that I experienced firsthand here.

    Pair it with some soju and beer. And make sure to also include some kimchi on the grill. Btw, the grill uses charcoal, and the management of both the fat with water and how clean it stays impressed me. Their marination doesn't abuse sugar like they do in America.

    Good BBQ, good price, fun place to bring friends. Come early. Oh, the soju is cheaper than water if you have lunch here.

    After your meal here, go for a walk. You’re walking distance to a beautiful park with the wall of the city, as well as brick buildings from major universities in Seoul. It’s really a beautiful walk and very necessary after the meal.

guest_review.author: Usagi
guest_review.intro: Mi amiga Usagi estuvo en Taipei y esto es lo que pensó de Shabu:
paragraphs: Me gustó este shabu mucho más que los de Japón. Todo se sentía más fresco, hasta orgánico. Que lleguen vivos los moluscos y el marisco le da un valor agregado, aunque sea un poco cruel. Te muestran los abalones moviéndose, los langostinos pidiendo ayuda, el cangrejo intentando huir. Luego se lo llevan y lo cortan. Yo no hubiera podido cortar el abalón entero. Demasiado cruel. Gracias por cortármelo.
Fue la primera vez que vi jamón ibérico en un shabu. En Japón no hay eso. Probamos el ibérico hervido. Un crimen en España, pero estaba rico, no me quejo.
En Japón el shabu lo haces tú. Acá metían todo, sacaban todo y te lo dejaban listo. Más relax. Por eso se sintió más high-class.

Recomiendo mucho el menú surf and turf: carne y mar. Éramos tres y con eso y el ibérico me llené. Calidad. Nunca había comido tomate en un shabu. Me sorprendió el postre: pudín, sandía, helado de matcha. En Japón, en un menú así, casi no viene.
No sentí necesidad de pedir más verduras ni más carne. Súper recomendado. Imagino que no fue barato. Por la experiencia, vale la pena.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
This is more than a review. It is a love letter to one of my favorite restaurants in the world.

I first tried Din Tai Fung in Hong Kong. In Kowloon I remember a branch with a Michelin star: one of those starred restaurants you actually had to try because it was affordable. I had no idea that this chain, and Taiwan itself, would become such a fun tradition in my life.

Din Tai Fung, or DTF: Down to Foodie. For me, it has become one of the flavors of Taiwan. Anyone who visits the island learns that locals really push this place. Friends in Taipei keep inviting me, and I usually let them order so I can learn what they love.

If you want the fancy location, there are a few in Xinyi. Taipei 101 (mall and observatory are mandatory) is busy. There is another one close by at A4. I dare you to try the original Xinyi Road shop in Da'an. That original is now takeaway-only. For dine-in, the Xinsheng flagship is across the street.

If you are elsewhere in the world, go to one of the big ones. The Las Vegas branch is one of my favorites: inside ARIA, on the casino floor, windows looking toward Vdara and Nancy Rubins' Big Edge, that large cactus-like sculpture. That view is part of what makes it fun. Westfield Valley Fair is the Bay Area mall branch, and where I occasionally end up for brunch. Los Angeles has many; Century City is one in a big mall, close after landing at LAX. There is still no San Francisco branch, which is fortunate: it stays something I look forward to when I travel.

In October 2026 I went to the Santa Monica Place branch. The Taiwanese cabbage was a very interesting surprise. Highly recommend it, and the wood ear mushrooms; they complement anything you order. For something different, get the kimchi and pork dumplings, unlike anything I've tried at other Din Tai Fungs.

In Taiwan I always go to Din Tai Fung. Get the xiaolongbao, the chilled cucumber salad with chili oil, and the soups. The hot-and-sour soup is amazing, and the chicken soup is really well done. Pot stickers are a must. Far from Taiwan, their boba tea is also good; in Taiwan, try other boba shops. Have the specialties at the restaurant, including the dessert xiaolongbao. They experiment with flavors and local stuff at many branches. It is always worth it.

Din Tai Fung is Taiwan. We should all try the flavors of this country. It has become a huge American business, but it still earns that loyalty. Worth it, and affordable for groups.

faqs.question: What should I order at El Chato?
faqs.answer: Go for the tapas, the tortilla española, and the wines. The tortilla is custardy inside and golden at the edges, served as a pintxo. I really enjoy the navajas, the jamón and cheese, and pan con tomate. Ask for chatos. Get vermut, including the non-alcoholic one if you are there early, or share an Estrella.

faqs.question: Does El Chato have non-alcoholic drinks?
faqs.answer: Yes. They have a great non-alcoholic vermut, which is what you want for those early World Cup matches.

faqs.question: Is there outdoor seating at El Chato?
faqs.answer: Yes. On a sunny day you can hang out outside on the corner of Bryant and 21st. The Mission gets better weather than the rest of the city, and that sidewalk is part of the vibe.

faqs.question: Is El Chato a restaurant or a bar?
faqs.answer: El Chato is a natural wine bar that serves excellent tapas. It is the kind of bar you end up trusting with a whole afternoon: come for the wine, stay for the tortilla española, and let the corner do the rest.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
This corner really makes Madrid a thing in the Mission. Beautiful place, great owners, and the kind of bar you end up trusting with a whole afternoon.

    Spending a lot of time in Madrid, Barcelona, Granada and San Sebastián, you develop a love for the passion of Spanish food. And finding that same character in their owners, that love for making a tortilla taste good and caring for the bread and the vermuts, that's what makes El Chato a place where you feel in España.

    It's a natural wine bar. Go for the tapas, the tortilla española, and the wines. They're just amazing. I really enjoy the navajas, and their jamón and cheese selection. Ask for some chatos so you can try more of what they have on the menu. The owners' passion shows in the food and in a list that leans on small European producers. The tortilla is simple, soft inside and golden at the edges.

    They serve that tortilla as a pintxo on grilled bread with piquillo and allioli. Get pan con tomate with it, and spread the tomato yourself. The toasted jamón sandwich with melted cheese and piparras is the other plate I keep in the middle of the table.

    During the World Cup this was a great community for following Spain. Locals and Spaniards hanging out, sharing an Estrella, calling the goals, passing around tortilla de patata and their vermut. They have a great non-alcoholic one for those early matches. The team is friendly. Trust their recommendations from the wine stand.

    On a sunny day (the Mission gets better weather than the rest of the city) you can hang out outside. That corner doesn't just feel Mission. A friend said it could be Roma in Mexico City, Castellana in Madrid, Palermo Soho in Buenos Aires, or Providencia in Chile. There's a vibe in the corner.

    Feels like a slice of Madrid in the Mission, with warm hospitality and flavors that actually hold up.

    A good friend invited me to try some of the local cuisine. I had some variation of this eating at another friend's house and also at a hawker market, but having the opportunity to explore a more interesting version of it in a beautiful setting is what attracted me to this place. And yes, the portions are big. The food is strong. I would say that after these we had to go for a walk and also a beautiful massage nearby. So yeah, this was really good food.

    The Singaporean flavors were there. I really enjoyed seeing how they cook some of this on leaves, reminding me of some of the Latin cuisine. Egg fried stuff, and of course the rice to love.

    It's also fascinating the location of the restaurant. It's close to Arab Street and Masjid Sultan, so you get to experience the variety and different approaches that Singapore has to offer. Great location, very nice atmosphere. Service was quick and the food came up very fast. I kind of feel like I got a kiss from Singapore with this beautiful meal.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
At Casa Escobar in Guatemala City, get the Mar y Tierra: lomito with giant shrimps.

Casa Escobar in the Cayalá city sits in the main area of the mall. Great location, where people like to hang out and eat. Great steak. They push international ingredients and methods: the puyazo (picanha) is from the US. Lomito comes both ways, US or local: ask for the local. It's really good. So is the local chorizo. They also do Argentinian chorizo made here following an Argentine recipe. Good wines from Argentina and Chile with the meat. Fast service, courses well timed, and they treat you properly. Fun with friends and family. Last visit was a big parrillada: carne adobada (pork), a bit dry but a different flavor, even if similar to Mexico. Also chicken, and tortillitas calientes. Consistent quality asado, carne asada the Guatemalan way. I recommend it.

Antigua was recently remodeled. Looks amazing. Nice service. One block from the parque central. Went back October 4, 2026 with friends. The Antigua location shines with the views to the ruins of La Compañía de Jesús. Good walk afterwards to the Spanish building, the Centro de Formación de la Cooperación Española, to check an exhibit.

Zona 10 / Guatemala City is more executive. Business during the week, families on weekends.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
If you read the fancy duck at Mister Jiu’s in San Francisco, this is where to go fancy in Taipei. Three Michelin stars. Gorgeous room. Decor, tables, lighting. Then the food. 17F, Palais de Chine, right on Taipei Main.

Order the duck with the reservation. Two ways: 先知鴨, the young duck, smaller, soft bone, usually two eats. Or 火焰片皮鴨, the flame crispy-skin duck, three or four ways, all the parts with max flavor. Book both days ahead.

Before even booking your flight ticket to Taipei, you should check if they have an opening at Le Palais. It will improve your trip and give you an amazing impression of how refined the food in Taiwan can be.

When the duck is ready, a chef brings it to your table and starts slicing. You’ll see that ritual all over the room, each table with its own chef. After the first serves, they turn the rest into soup. You get a few choices. We also had the fried rice. Nice. Their teas are delightful.

My duck place in Taiwan. Been a couple of times for important celebrations. Always a must when bringing friends to the city. Pair it with the museum, the pork and the jade cabbage, and you get why this city is full of foodies.

Then go cheap. Night market duck: 金馥記脆皮烤鴨 in Shilin, and 真福記 in Songshan near Taipei Arena. Hotel one night, daily meal the next. What a city. Always underrated. Good for the ones who know.

If you love Korean BBQ, this is the fancy version in San Francisco. You will be full, you will be happy, and you can get leftover food to go. I always enjoy going with friends to a Korean barbecue, but for an upscale experience, San Ho Won is the one you're looking for if you want to impress. Not only will they make great barbecue meat for you, but their selection of beverages and add-ons is superb. If you've ever gone to a Korean barbecue and were worried about overcooking the meat or not having it at the right point, that's what San Ho Won will do for you.

Reservations are hard to get in advance unless you want to try the last serving at night, and that late seating might be a heavy meal. Still, San Ho Won is a very good deal: a Michelin-star menu, a very good selection of meat, and a reservation that is worth sharing with a group of four or even six people. Plan ahead, and sometimes check for the very last options in the schedule because they tend to open up occasionally. This is definitely a place worth visiting in San Francisco.

faqs.answer: Yes. The restaurant at Il San Pietro di Positano is Zass. I wrote Zaas on the original reel; the official name is Zass.

faqs.answer: It is just outside of Positano, at Il San Pietro in Laurito. That is the point: the view, the hotel, and a quieter cliff above the town.

faqs.question: Do I need a reservation at Zass in Positano?
faqs.answer: Yes. Book through the hotel. Online tables open 30 days ahead at 9am local time (2026), and groups larger than four should call. It is Michelin-starred, and the terrace fills up.

faqs.question: What should I order at Zass?
faqs.answer: If you skip the tasting menu, go for the pastas. Start with the octopus and figs. Get the lemon tagliatelle with lobster and pistachios, the spaghetti, and the cannelloni with ricotta and basil. Share a local fish, and do not skip the mini crème brûlée.

faqs.question: Is Zass only for hotel guests?
faqs.answer: No. Outside guests can reserve. Dress smart casual: long trousers, no shorts or sneakers. The terrace over the sea cliff is the whole point.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
Nothing screams "jet set" more than a meal at Zass, located in the hotel Il San Pietro di Positano.

Just outside of Positano, this is the perfect romantic place for fine dining. The view, the location, the lovely hotel, and the beautiful presentation and flavors.

The terrace looks over the sea cliff. The restaurant grows its own vegetables in the hotel garden, and a pizza oven stands at one end. Piano music in the air, and staff who actually make you comfortable.

They offer a tasting menu with wine pairings. We skipped it and went for the pastas. We started with a fish tartare, but the true star was the octopus with figs.

And then there was pasta. The spaghetti was impeccable. The tagliatelle, infused with lemon, accented by lobster and pistachios, ranks among the best we have ever tasted. The cannelloni, rich with ricotta and basil, is not something to skip.

We finished sharing a local fish. We almost skipped dessert, then they brought candies and a mini crème brûlée I can still taste with my eyes closed.

We did a small reel when we visited. Check it out.

Thank you for the enchanting evening, Zass.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
Diacá, Cuatro Grados Norte: bring grandpa to the tasting menu.

Tasting menu in Guatemala, in a beautiful location in Cuatro Grados. To try this place, I brought my grandpa. Half of the fun was to enjoy good Guatemalan food with him. And this was his first tasting menu. He asked a few times to repeat some dishes. They were confused. He also wondered if they were going to interrupt our conversation every time they brought another dish.

They do a lot of local dishes and also a brunch menu when I visited. A sausage of beans, really good eggs (huevitos revueltos chapines) and a lot of ingredients that will trigger your childhood if you were born in this country. A good tasting menu to share with international friends looking to explore la tierra de la eterna primavera.

Chef Débora Fadul is really building something special here. Diacá means de acá, from here. They later moved from the Cuatro Grados tower out to Muxbal, and made Latin America's 50 Best in 2025.
reviews.reservation_tip: Book ahead. This review is from December 2022 at the old Cuatro Grados tower; the restaurant is now in Muxbal (Final 20 Calle km 8, Carretera a Muxbal).

faqs.answer: They do a tasting menu of local dishes, and when I visited they also had a brunch menu. Look for the sausage of beans and the huevitos revueltos chapines: really good eggs and ingredients that will trigger your childhood if you were born in Guatemala.

reviews.personal_recommendation:
Plow, the definite place for brunch in San Francisco.

Every time somebody asks me where to go for brunch, I mention Plow. I really like the place. It’s a great destination on Potrero Hill, and you’ll always find a line on a busy day. Go on a Wednesday, or get there early, and you can get in. It’s definitely worth it. Behind the bar, happy cooks are always surprising you with breakfasts: eggs, bread, and sometimes a Chinese version of breakfast. It’s always a fantastic experience. The coffee, the ambience, and the flavors. Try the different menus and see what you like.

Plow’s great. It’s worth the wait. If the line is really hard, still put your name on the list, walk to Farley’s (1315 18th St) half a block away, grab a tea or a coffee, and come back. I’ve had some of the best conversations in that line. If you’re lucky, you’re just getting in. I still remember during the pandemic they kept serving breakfast. I’m not sure about delivery, but I remember picking up directly. They always handed over those packages with a great smile and a lot of thanks. Plow is where you go for breakfast and really enjoy it. That’s why San Francisco has spots that are worth it. This is my best example.

Try to avoid weekends. It’s super crowded. Get there early on a weekday and you’ll have the best experience.
